title: Four Classic Sadya Recipes to Bring Kerala's Onam Feast to Your Table
excerpt: With Thiruvonam just days away on August 26, these traditional vegetarian recipes — cabbage thoran, cheera parippu, avial, and sambar — capture the essence of Kerala's grandest meal.
body:
• Onam 2026 culminates with Thiruvonam on August 26, when families across Kerala and the global diaspora gather for the traditional Sadya feast served on banana leaves.
  • A complete Sadya can include 26 to 30 dishes balancing sweet, sour, salty, spicy, bitter, and savoury flavours in a single sitting.
  • Four foundational recipes — cabbage thoran, cheera parippu, avial, and sambar — form the backbone of any home Sadya and can be prepared with ingredients available at most Indian grocery stores abroad.
  • The feast is entirely vegetarian, rooted in Kerala's harvest traditions, and observed across religious communities as a secular cultural celebration.

The Festival Behind the Feast

Onam is Kerala's ten-day harvest festival, celebrated during Chingam, the first month of the Malayalam calendar. It marks the mythical annual homecoming of King Mahabali, a just ruler whose reign is remembered as a golden age of equality and prosperity. This year, celebrations began on August 16 with Atham and culminate with Thiruvonam on August 26, the festival's most important day.

While Onam has Hindu roots, it has evolved into a secular cultural celebration observed across religious communities in Kerala and by Malayalis around the world. Households lay out intricate floral carpets called Pookalam, participate in traditional games, and — at the heart of it all — sit down together for the Onam Sadya, a multi-course vegetarian banquet served on banana leaves.

What Goes on a Banana Leaf

Sadhya means "feast" in Malayalam, and there is no single definitive version. A modest spread might contain fewer than ten dishes; elaborate celebrations can feature thirty or more. The meal is built around balance — sweet, sour, salty, spicy, bitter, and savoury flavours arrive together with contrasting textures on a single leaf, according to Chef Sandeep Ail of Punjab Grill UAE, who described the philosophy to The National.

Diners eat with their right hand, traditionally starting with rice, parippu, and ghee, then progressing through sambar, rasam, and an array of vegetable preparations, pickles, and chutneys before finishing with payasam desserts. Below are four foundational recipes that anchor the feast.

Cabbage Thoran

A dry stir-fry of shredded cabbage with grated coconut, thoran is one of the Sadya's essential vegetable preparations. Heat coconut oil and crackle mustard seeds, then add dry red chillies, curry leaves, sliced shallots, slit green chillies, and julienned ginger. Sauté for two minutes before adding shredded cabbage, a pinch of turmeric, and salt. Cook on high heat until the cabbage softens, then finish with freshly grated coconut. The recipe, shared by Chef Ashwani Kumar Singh of The Leela Ambience Convention Hotel, takes under fifteen minutes and yields a crunchy, coconut-fragrant side that pairs with rice and sambar.

Cheera Parippu

This comforting lentil-and-spinach preparation brings protein and greens to the banana leaf. Boil tuvar dal until soft, then separately sauté onions and garlic in oil until golden. Add chopped tomatoes and cook until they break down, followed by shredded spinach, ginger, green chillies, and salt. Combine the cooked dal with the spinach mixture and bring to a boil. Finish with a tempering of mustard seeds, cumin seeds, and dry red chillies crackled in ghee. Pour the tempering into the dal and serve hot.

Avial

Perhaps the dish most closely associated with Sadya, avial brings together multiple vegetables — pumpkin, yam, raw banana, ash gourd, and snake beans — in a coconut and cumin paste finished with curry leaves and coconut oil. Cut all vegetables into batons and cook them in water with salt until half-done. Separately grind grated coconut, green chillies, and cumin seeds into a coarse paste. Add turmeric to the vegetables, stir in the coconut paste, and simmer until everything is fully cooked. Finish with beaten curd, a tempering of mustard seeds and dry red chillies in coconut oil, and cover to let the flavours infuse.

"The idea is not to reinvent the feast, but to understand what makes it special — the balance of flavours, the order in which the meal unfolds and, most importantly, the sense of abundance and togetherness that defines Onam."

— Sandeep Ail, Brand Executive Chef, Punjab Grill UAE

Sambar

The Sadya's heartiest curry, sambar combines toor dal with a medley of vegetables — carrots, drumstick, brinjal, ash gourd, and pearl onions — in a tamarind-spice base. Pressure cook the dal until soft. Separately, soak tamarind to extract juice, then boil it with the vegetables, green chillies, curry leaves, and salt until tender. Add the cooked dal and a spice powder ground from roasted cumin, fenugreek, and coriander seeds, along with chilli powder, turmeric, coriander powder, and a pinch of asafoetida. Simmer for five minutes, then finish with a coconut oil tempering of mustard seeds, dried red chillies, chopped shallots, and curry leaves.

Bringing the Feast Home

For diaspora families, recreating a Sadya far from Kerala can be a powerful act of cultural connection. Most ingredients — coconut oil, curry leaves, tamarind, toor dal, and fresh coconut — are available at Indian grocery stores across the United States, United Kingdom, and Middle East. Kerala community organisations in major global hubs plan to host public banquets and cultural showcases throughout late August, timed around weekends for working families.

The Kerala government has declared four consecutive public holidays from August 25 through August 28. Tourism Minister P.C. Vishnunath has announced expanded festival programming in Thiruvananthapuram, including a dedicated Festival Zone from Kowdiar to Manacaud and performances of rare ritual art forms like Padayani, Theyyam, and Tholpavakoothu.

Whether prepared at home or enjoyed at a community gathering, the Sadya remains one of India's great culinary traditions — a meal designed not just to feed, but to celebrate abundance, togetherness, and the turning of the harvest season.
